locations.name: Pittman's Gas and Service
locations.description: Four pumps under a buzzing canopy where the state highway meets the river road, with a bus-stop sign bolted to the ice machine and a hand-lettered board out front that reads CRICKETS, NIGHT CRAWLERS, CARTONS. Out back, two open service bays smell of hot oil and tire rubber, and a radio plays gospel to whatever truck is up on the lift.
locations.details: The counter sells crickets, cartons, scratch-offs, boiled peanuts and two-dollar coffee under Clyde Pittman's photo, and a flyer on the door calls the town to the council's bridge vote on Tuesday, October 13. Lamar Haskins drinks his coffee by the window most mornings, and Kaylee Pittman works the register after school.
locations.hours: 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. every day; the service bays close at 5
locations.history: Clyde Pittman built the station in 1966, when the highway still brought the trucks through town, and Royce took it over when his daddy died at the pumps in 2009.

locations.name: The Low Water
locations.description: A cinderblock bar on Front Street with neon beer signs in the window, a pool table with a slow lean and a flood line drawn in marker beside the door. On weekends the gravel lot fills with car tags from the dry county, and the kitchen hatch at the back sends out catfish baskets and the smell of old fryer grease.
locations.details: A beer is three dollars, a catfish basket nine, and the jukebox still takes quarters. Dollar bills signed by regulars are stapled over the bar, and the card game runs at the back table most nights under a lamp nobody else sits under.
locations.hours: 11 a.m. to 2 a.m., Monday to Saturday; closed Sundays
locations.history: Loretta Gaddis bought the Low Water in 1994, the year the bypass opened, and has kept it open through every flood since; the marker line by the door is from April 2025.

locations.name: The Riverview Motor Court
locations.description: Twelve rooms in a single-story L around a cracked parking lot, under a sign that says VACANCY in every season and a name that promises a view you only get from behind the dumpster. The office smells of burnt coffee and air freshener, and a monitor on the counter shows the lot in four gray squares.
locations.details: A room is forty-nine dollars a night or two hundred a week, cash preferred. Lyman Coker, Leon Varner and Curtis Pruett rent theirs by the week, and Boyd Teague has had Room 9 since last week. The office has a coffee pot and a bell nobody answers before dark.
locations.hours: Office open 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.; checkout at 11
locations.history: The Riverview went up in 1962 for the highway trade and has had five owners since the bypass took the trucks away; Stanley Wexler bought it in 2019.

locations.name: Riverside Baptist Church
locations.description: A white clapboard church on the slope above Front Street, with a steeple that leans a little toward the river and a marquee sign out front that reads PRAY FOR OUR BRIDGE. Inside, the pews smell of lemon polish and old hymnals, and the fellowship hall out back keeps a coffee urn and a box of donated coats going all week.
locations.details: Thirty pews, the piano Nadine Dees plays every Sunday, and a board in the fellowship hall with the prayer list and the pantry schedule. The coffee is free, and the coats in the box by the door are for whoever needs one.
locations.hours: Sunday school 9:45, service at 11; supper and prayer Wednesdays at 6
locations.history: Riverside Baptist was built in 1911 on land the Gentrys gave, and Ray Dees has been its pastor since 1994; the new roof went on this summer.

locations.name: Town Hall
locations.description: A two-story brick building with the mayor's office upstairs and the police department downstairs, one patrol car out front and a second up on blocks behind it. The station is a front counter, three desks and a single holding cell, and the window unit drips onto a box of unpaid parking tickets.
locations.details: Upstairs is the council room with its folding chairs and the mayor's office; downstairs is the station, three desks, a holding cell with a steel bench and a coffee maker older than Officer Ballard. A board by the door posts the council agendas and the parking fines.
locations.hours: Clerk's office 8 to 4:30 on weekdays; the police answer the door day and night
locations.history: Town Hall went up in 1956, when the town still had money, and the police department moved into its ground floor in 1978.

locations.name: Byrd's Pawn
locations.description: A narrow storefront between two empty ones, its window crowded with chainsaws, guitars and fishing reels behind a security grille that never goes all the way up. Inside it smells of gun oil and stale smoke, and a glass counter of rings and phones sits under a hand-lettered sign that says NO REFUNDS NO STORIES.
locations.details: Chainsaws, guitars, rifles, fishing reels and wedding rings, each with a paper tag and a price Hollis will argue about. Loans run thirty days at twenty-five percent, and the back room is off limits.
locations.history: Hollis Byrd opened the pawn shop in 1988 in what had been the auto parts store, and it is the last store open on its side of Front Street.

locations.name: Riverbend Trailer Park
locations.description: Thirty-odd trailers on the low ground downstream of the landing, some with flower boxes and some with blue tarps on the roofs, strung along a gravel loop that floods to the axles every spring. Dogs bark on chains, a trampoline rusts in the middle of the loop, and a cross of plastic flowers is wired to the fence by the mailboxes.
locations.details: Lot rent is two hundred and fifty a month, paid into a Sturdivant Land and Timber box at the gate. June Satterfield's porch light stays on all night, Shayla Rawls does hair in her trailer for fifteen dollars, and the cross by the mailboxes is for Amber Lott.
locations.history: Riverbend was a fish camp until 1974, when the Sturdivants cut it into trailer lots; it floods every spring and went under to the windows in April 2025.

locations.name: Purvis Landing
locations.description: A bait shop on stilts, a fuel pump and a floating dock of aluminum johnboats and bass boats, beside the concrete public ramp that runs straight down into the water. At night the dock lights stay off, and every morning the mud at the foot of the ramp is cut with fresh trailer tracks.
locations.details: Crickets are three dollars a tube, minnows four dollars a dozen and gas a quarter over the station's price. Lorna Purvis keeps the shop, and Burl Satterfield fixes outboards on the dock in the afternoons. A flyer taped to the drink cooler calls the town to the council's bridge vote on Tuesday, October 13.
locations.hours: 5 a.m. to 7 p.m.; the ramp is open all night
locations.history: The Purvis family has run the landing since 1952 on land leased from the Sturdivants, at the spot where the Gentry ferry used to tie up.

locations.name: Sturdivant House
locations.description: A white two-story house with eight columns on the hill above town, its lawn mowed in stripes and its paint peeling on the side nobody sees from the road. At the end of the drive by the water tower you can get the town's one bar of cell signal, which is why so many trucks go up past the house after dark.
locations.details: Portraits of three generations of Sturdivants line the stairs, the parlor smells of furniture wax and old roses, and the clocks all run a little slow. Odessa Fairley answers the door and decides who gets past it.
locations.hours: Callers by invitation; Miss Vada receives in the evening
locations.history: Amos Sturdivant built the house in 1926, and Vada was born in its front bedroom in 1946.

locations.name: The Old Bridge
locations.description: A narrow green steel truss from 1938, two lanes and no shoulder, posted at five tons and rattling under every pickup that crosses toward the dry county. Halfway over, a sign on the rail marks the state line, and Virgil Odom fishes off the concrete pier below the first span most afternoons.
locations.details: A bronze plaque at the town end names the 1938 highway commission and Amos Sturdivant. The deck rattles under every truck, the rail is scratched with initials and dates, and the pier below the first span is the best catfish hole on this stretch of river.
locations.history: The bridge opened in October 1938 after Amos Sturdivant's three-year fight with the state, put the Gentry ferry out of business, and has been posted at five tons since 2019.

locations.name: Front Street
locations.description: Two blocks of brick storefronts between the Low Water and Byrd's Pawn, most of them empty, with plywood over the windows of the old drugstore and the old bank. Halfway down, Wiley Tackett's garage sits with its bay doors chained under a faded sign that still says TACKETT AUTO REPAIR.
locations.details: The empty garage has a for-sale sign from Sturdivant Land and Timber in the office window and an oil stain in each bay. The old bank's vault door still shows through the plywood, and Elbert Gentry and Burl Satterfield sit on the bench outside the old drugstore most mornings.
locations.history: Front Street was the main street when the trucks still came through, and its stores closed one at a time after the bypass opened in 1994.

locations.name: Riverside Cemetery
locations.description: A sloping acre beside Riverside Baptist with cedar trees, a chain-link fence and graves going back to the 1840s, the oldest with their names worn off. The newest is a mound of red clay under a metal funeral-home marker, covered in plastic flowers and a stuffed bear.
locations.details: Amber Lott's grave is the fresh one by the back fence, and Ruth Haskins lies under a stone with room on it for Lamar. Amos Sturdivant has the tallest monument, a gray obelisk, and Tammy Lott sits by Amber's grave most mornings before her shift.
locations.history: The town buried its dead here before there was a church to bury them from, and the Gentrys, the Sturdivants and the Pittmans each have a corner.

locations.name: The Water Tower
locations.description: A silver tank on four legs at the top of the hill above town, with the town's name painted around it and a gravel turnaround at its feet where the Sturdivant drive ends. Stand by the fence and your phone finds one bar, which is the whole reason anybody drives up here.
locations.details: Beer cans and cigarette butts in the gravel, initials painted on the legs, and a view of the bridge, the river and the lights of the dry county. After dark Kaylee Pittman drives her daddy's truck up here most nights for the signal.
locations.history: The town put the tower up in 1964 and painted it every ten years until the money ran out; the class of 2019 painted over the last coat.

locations.name: The Bluff
locations.description: A pull-off on the state highway at the top of the bluff, where the road comes out of the pine woods and drops toward Pittman's in two switchbacks. A green sign by the guardrail says LOCKETT'S FERRY POP 812, and from the rail you can see the whole town, the bridge and the river bending away downstream.
locations.details: A historical marker about the Gentry ferry stands by the guardrail, half hidden in kudzu. Log trucks downshift loud here all night, and Travis Cagle parks the patrol car behind the sign to run radar at the start of his shift.
locations.history: The highway came down the bluff in 1938 to meet the new bridge, and the state widened the switchbacks in 1971 after a log truck went over the rail.

locations.name: The River Road
locations.description: A two-lane blacktop that leaves the highway at Pittman's and follows the river upstream past the Mangum House, a string of fish camps and a row of mailboxes on posts. It has no shoulder and deep ditches, and the deer come out on it at dusk.
locations.details: A hand-painted sign for fresh eggs, a speed limit sign shot full of holes and a low spot past the Mangum House where the water crosses every spring. Nikki Ballard runs it every morning.
locations.history: It was the wagon road to the upriver fish camps long before the bridge, and the county paved it in 1961 as far as the last camp.

locations.name: The Mangum House
locations.description: A white frame house about a mile up the river road from Pittman's, on the left, with a carport full of engine parts and a porch light left on for whoever gets home last. In the daytime it is dim and quiet, blackout curtains drawn over the bedroom where Mavis sleeps off the night shift.
locations.details: The front room is still Inez's, with her plastic-covered sofa and church fans, and the kitchen is Dewayne's, with engine parts soaking in the sink. The blackout curtains in the back bedroom stay shut all day.
locations.history: It was Inez Crocker's house for forty years; her daughter Mavis and Dewayne Mangum moved in to look after her in 2021 and stayed after she died.

locations.name: The Pittman Place
locations.description: A brick ranch house up the bluff behind the station, with a basketball hoop over the garage, a bass boat on a trailer and the station's ledgers spread across the kitchen table. The curtains are always half shut, and from the back steps you can see every truck that stops at the pumps.
locations.details: Kaylee's softball trophies fill the den, the kitchen table is covered in the station's ledgers, and the living room curtains are always half shut. The bass boat in the drive has not been in the water since spring.
locations.history: Royce and Darlene Pittman built the ranch house in 1998 on a lot behind the station that Clyde Pittman gave them as a wedding present.

locations.name: The Parsonage
locations.description: A small white house beside Riverside Baptist that the church owns, with a porch swing, a vegetable garden gone to seed and the church van parked on the grass. Inside it smells of coffee and cough drops, and the front room is stacked with boxes of canned goods for the pantry.
locations.details: The front room is stacked with canned goods for the pantry, and Micah has his mother's old room at the back. Nadine keeps a pot of coffee on from six in the morning.
locations.hours: A private home; the pastor answers the door at any hour
locations.history: The church built the parsonage in 1952, and the Dees family has lived in it since Ray took the pulpit in 1994.

locations.name: The Lott Trailer
locations.description: A single-wide at the far end of the Riverbend loop, with a wind chime of bent spoons on the porch and a girl's pink bicycle chained to the steps that nobody rides now. A handmade sign taped inside the front window says JUSTICE FOR AMBER in marker.
locations.details: Amber's photos are taped all around the TV, her room is the way she left it, and the kitchen smells of fryer grease from Tammy's work shirts. A coffee can by the door collects money for a headstone.
locations.history: Tammy Lott has rented the single-wide since 2008, and Amber grew up in its front bedroom.

locations.name: The Apartment over Byrd's
locations.description: Two rooms up an outside staircase above Byrd's Pawn, rented by the month, with a dripping window unit, a police radio on the counter and a view straight down into the alley where trucks stop after dark. The landlord's boxes of unclaimed merchandise still fill the hall closet.
locations.details: Rent is four hundred a month, and Hollis collects it in person. The window unit drips into a bucket, the police radio is never off, and the only thing on the walls is a framed academy photo of Nikki in uniform.
locations.history: Hollis Byrd raised his daughter Renee in these two rooms and has rented them by the month since she left; Nikki Ballard moved in two years ago.

locations.name: The Haskins Farm
locations.description: A tin-roofed farmhouse at the end of a gravel road north of town, with a grain truck under the shed, soybean stubble out to the tree line and a hand-painted sign by the mailbox that once said NO NEW BRIDGE and has been painted over. The kitchen table is covered in seed bills and a county map with the downstream bridge route drawn on it in pencil.
locations.details: Ruth Haskins's recipe cards are still in a tin by the stove, and Virgil Odom's tackle and old bridge reports fill the back porch. Seed bills are stuck to the refrigerator with feed store magnets.
locations.history: The Haskins family has farmed here since 1931 and has leased the Sturdivant bottomland since 1960.

locations.name: The Overstreet House
locations.description: A neat yellow house on the rise behind Town Hall, with a flag on the porch, a scanner squawking in the front window and a chest freezer humming in the carport. The front room is full of the mayor's binders and council minutes, and somebody is always home.
locations.details: Council binders cover the dining table, the scanner in the window is never off, and Gerald's mill union plaques hang in the hall. The chest freezer in the carport is full of deer meat.
locations.history: Gerald and Jolene Overstreet bought the yellow house in 1991, the year they married, and Annette moved back into her old room in 2022.

locations.name: The Gentry House
locations.description: The oldest house in town, a gray two-story with a deep porch on the slope between the church and Front Street, built by the family that ran the ferry before there was a bridge. Photographs of the river in flood cover every wall, and three rocking chairs on the porch face the water.
locations.details: Every wall is covered in photographs of the river in flood, each labeled with the year and the height in Elbert's hand. The house smells of pipe smoke and mothballs, and Pearl's newspaper clippings fill a whole bedroom.
locations.hours: A private home; Elbert is on the porch most evenings
locations.history: Asa Gentry built the house in 1890 with ferry money, and it is the oldest building in town; Elbert was born in it in 1938, the year the ferry ended.

locations.name: Clayburn
locations.distance: twenty-six miles north up the state highway, about forty minutes by car
locations.description: The county seat, a town of six thousand around a domed courthouse, with the sheriff's office in its basement, a grocery, two banks and the county home. People from Lockett's Ferry drive up for court dates, paperwork, school and anything a gas station does not sell.
locations.details: The courthouse square has a diner, a pharmacy and two banks, and the title-loan office is out on the highway with repossessed trucks behind it. The county home is four blocks off the square, and the county school is on the north edge of town.
locations.history: Clayburn took the county seat from Lockett's Ferry in an election in 1871, and Elbert Gentry still says it was stolen.

locations.name: The Sheriff's Office
locations.distance: in the courthouse basement in Clayburn, twenty-six miles north
locations.description: The county sheriff's office and jail in the basement of the Clayburn courthouse, with a front counter behind thick glass and twenty-two beds in the jail behind it. Eleven deputies cover the whole county from here, and it takes one of them an hour or more to reach Lockett's Ferry.
locations.details: Wanted posters, a coffee machine and a sign-in book for jail visitors. The dispatcher answers the phone with the sheriff's campaign slogan.
locations.history: Sheriff Hoyt Bramlett has run it since 2006, and his deputies and the Lockett's Ferry police have not trusted each other since an arrest at the bridge went wrong in 2011.

locations.name: The County Home
locations.distance: four blocks off the courthouse square in Clayburn, twenty-six miles north
locations.description: The county nursing home, a one-story brick building in Clayburn with sixty beds, a dayroom television that is never off and a lot full of aides' cars. In Lockett's Ferry, going to the county home means you have nobody left.
locations.details: The halls smell of disinfectant and cafeteria gravy, and the visiting hours are taped to the door.
locations.history: It opened in 1968 to replace the county poor farm and has been short of staff every year since.

locations.name: The County School
locations.distance: on the north edge of Clayburn, fifty minutes on the school bus
locations.description: The county's middle and high school together, two long brick wings and a football field on the north edge of Clayburn, with eleven hundred students. The bus for Lockett's Ferry leaves the Riverbend mailboxes at ten to seven.
locations.details: Annette Overstreet teaches seventh grade in the middle school wing, and Kaylee Pittman pitches for the softball team. The trophy case by the gym has one plaque with a Lockett's Ferry name on it.
locations.history: Children from Lockett's Ferry have ridden the bus to Clayburn since 1987.

locations.name: The Old County Hospital
locations.distance: on the south side of Clayburn, twenty-six miles north
locations.description: A three-story brick hospital in Clayburn with its windows boarded and its sign taken down, closed since 2019. Since it shut, the nearest emergency room has been Calder Regional, forty miles away.
locations.details: The parking lot is fenced and the ambulance bay is chained. A banner on the fence still says THANK YOU HEALTHCARE HEROES.
locations.history: It opened in 1952, delivered most of the people in Lockett's Ferry under seventy, and closed in March 2019 when the company that bought it went bankrupt; June Satterfield nursed there for twenty-six years.

locations.name: Calder
locations.distance: forty miles north, past Clayburn on the state highway, about an hour
locations.description: The city, as people in Lockett's Ferry say it: forty thousand people, a regional hospital, lawyers, doctors, a mall and a treatment center. Anyone who leaves Lockett's Ferry for good seems to end up here first.
locations.details: The courthouse square has the law offices and a private lender's office over a bank, and the hospital and the clinics are out by the interstate.
locations.history: Calder grew on the railroad and the paper trade, and it has been taking Lockett's Ferry's young people and business for sixty years.

locations.name: Calder Regional
locations.distance: forty miles north in Calder, an hour by car and longer by ambulance
locations.description: The regional medical center in Calder, with the nearest emergency room to Lockett's Ferry, a helicopter pad and a waiting room that is full every night. The ambulance from Clayburn takes an hour to get to the river and another to get back.
locations.details: The emergency room has forty chairs and a vending machine, and the night nurses know June Satterfield's voice from years of phone calls.
locations.hours: Emergency room open day and night
locations.history: It took over the county's patients when the old county hospital closed in 2019.

locations.name: The Willows
locations.distance: on the edge of Calder, forty miles north
locations.description: A treatment center for drugs and alcohol on the edge of Calder, in an old motel with a fence around it and a garden the patients keep. It has a waiting list of three months and allows one phone call a week.
locations.details: Sunday visits are in the dayroom from 1 to 4, with coffee in paper cups and a wall of photos of the people who finished.
locations.history: It opened in 2015 in the old Willows motel and is where families from three counties send the people they cannot help any more.

locations.name: The State Penitentiary
locations.distance: a hundred and forty miles north, three hours each way
locations.description: The state's maximum-security prison, cellblocks and cotton fields behind two fences in the flat country to the north. Visiting is the second and fourth Saturday, and the trip from Lockett's Ferry takes all day.
locations.details: The visiting room has vending machines, plastic chairs and a guard at each door. A collect call costs three dollars for fifteen minutes.
locations.hours: Visiting the second and fourth Saturday, 9 to 3
locations.history: Half the men in Lockett's Ferry over fifty know someone who did time there, and Dale Purvis has been there since 2018.

locations.name: The Sturdivant Bottomland
locations.distance: five miles downstream by the county road past Riverbend, ten minutes by truck
locations.description: Two thousand acres of flat river bottom five miles downstream, soybeans and cotton out to the tree line, where the state would build the new bridge if the council picks the downstream site. Survey stakes with orange flags run across the fields to the water.
locations.details: A gravel farm road runs down to the river past the forty acres the Haskins family owns outright, the soybean stubble is cut close, and a culvert by the road marks where the new interchange would go.
locations.history: Amos Sturdivant bought the bottomland in 1924, and the Haskins family has farmed it on a lease since 1960.

locations.name: The Sturdivant Timber
locations.distance: upriver and inland, twenty to forty minutes by logging road
locations.description: Eleven thousand acres of planted pine upriver and inland, cut on a thirty-year rotation by Sturdivant Land and Timber's crews. Logging roads, a skidder yard and a deer camp are about all there is out there.
locations.details: The skidder yard smells of diesel and cut pine, the deer camp has a sign-in board, and a white cross for Harlan Voss is nailed to a pine at the yard gate.
locations.hours: Crews work dawn to dusk, six days a week
locations.history: Harlan Voss bought most of it in the 1980s and died out there in 2014; Dwight Spann's crew cuts it now.

locations.name: The Old Paper Mill
locations.distance: nine miles downstream by the county road past Riverbend
locations.description: A closed paper mill nine miles downstream, a mile of rusting sheds, smokestacks and settling ponds behind a fence with the company's name painted out. It employed four hundred people until it shut in 2016.
locations.details: The gate has a scrapper's padlock, the guard shack windows are broken, and the union hall across the road is a church now.
locations.history: The mill opened in 1958 and kept Lockett's Ferry going for fifty years; Gerald Overstreet ran its paper machines for thirty-three of them.

locations.name: The Bypass
locations.distance: twelve miles east; the long way round to the dry county takes forty minutes
locations.description: The four-lane highway that runs north and south twelve miles east of town, with the nearest other bridge over the Lusk. It is why the trucks stopped coming through Lockett's Ferry, and if the old bridge closes it is how everyone will get to the dry county.
locations.details: A truck stop, a fireworks stand and a weigh station at the exit, and a billboard for a lawyer in Calder.
locations.history: It opened in 1994 after a fight that split the council three to two; Loretta Gaddis and Clyde Pittman led the side that lost.

locations.name: The Dry County
locations.distance: across the old bridge, over the state line
locations.description: The county across the river in the next state, dry since 1907, with a cigarette tax twice this side's and a sheriff who does not come across. Its people drive over the old bridge for beer, cartons and the Low Water.
locations.details: Its first gas station is a mile past the bridge and sells nothing stronger than root beer.
locations.history: It voted itself dry in 1907, and somebody in Lockett's Ferry has made money on the difference ever since.

locations.name: The Coast
locations.distance: three hundred miles down the river, a long day's drive
locations.description: Where the Lusk meets the Gulf, three hundred miles downriver: casinos, condos, shrimp boats and the place people in Lockett's Ferry talk about retiring to. The towboats that pass the old bridge end their runs there.
locations.details: Nobody from Lockett's Ferry lives there yet.
locations.history: Towboats have run down the river to the coast since before the bridge, and the deckhands still talk about it as the end of the line.

memories.text: bought me a beer at the bar

npcs.name: Loretta Gaddis
npcs.role: owner and bartender of the Low Water
npcs.look: Rail-thin woman of sixty with frosted hair, reading glasses on a beaded chain and a bar towel over one shoulder.
npcs.voice: Flat and unhurried; calls everybody 'hon', answers a question she doesn't like by asking what you're drinking, and never says a name out loud if she can point instead.
npcs.goal: Keep the old bridge open, because half her trade drives over from the dry county and none of it will drive the long way round.
npcs.secret: She has been seeing Royce Pittman on Tuesday afternoons for eleven years, and she is the reason he has not promised his vote to Carter Sturdivant.
npcs.history: Loretta Gaddis grew up at Riverbend, tended bar in Calder in her twenties and came home in 1991. She and Clyde Pittman led the losing side of the bypass fight, and she bought the Low Water in 1994, the year the bypass opened, with what she had saved. She lives in the two rooms behind the bar and has kept it open through every flood since.

memories.text: called me a liar in my own station

npcs.name: Royce Pittman
npcs.role: owner of Pittman's Gas and Service and the swing vote on the town council
npcs.look: Big, soft-bellied man in his fifties in a feed-store cap and a short-sleeved dress shirt, with a pen behind each ear.
npcs.voice: Folksy and slippery; dodges a straight answer, now and then with a story about his daddy; once in a while hedges with 'now, I'm not saying'; laughs to fill a silence.
npcs.goal: Get out from under the note on his station without having to pick a side where anybody can see him do it.
npcs.secret: Carter Sturdivant holds the note on the station and has offered to tear it up and give him the truck stop lease at the new interchange in return for a yes vote.
npcs.history: Royce Pittman grew up behind the counter of the station his daddy built and took it over when Clyde Pittman died at the pumps in 2009. He has sat on the town council for twelve years and is known for never saying how he will vote until he has to. He coaches Kaylee's softball team in the spring.

npcs.name: Vada Sturdivant
npcs.role: widow who owns Sturdivant House and the bottomland downstream
npcs.look: Small, straight-backed woman of eighty in a cardigan and pearls, with garden dirt under her nails and a cane she points with more than she leans on.
npcs.voice: Crisp and formal, with an old schoolteacher's diction; calls grown men 'son', corrects your grammar mid-sentence, and answers questions about money by asking who your people are.
npcs.goal: Keep the old bridge her father fought the state for in 1938, and keep the bottomland out of Carter's hands while she is alive.
npcs.secret: The Sturdivant money started with her father running whiskey into the dry county, and Wade Purvis still brings her an envelope every month, which is why the landing lease has never gone up.
npcs.history: Vada Sturdivant was born in Sturdivant House in 1946, the daughter of Amos Sturdivant, and taught school in Clayburn for thirty years. She married Harlan Voss in 1977, kept her own name and gave it to their son, and has been a widow since 2014. The house, the hill and the bottomland are still in her name.

npcs.name: Carter Sturdivant
npcs.role: head of Sturdivant Land and Timber, who holds half the town's paper
npcs.look: Trim, tanned man of forty-five in a quarter-zip pullover and pressed khakis, turning a truck key fob over and over in his fingers.
npcs.voice: Fast and friendly, like a salesman closing; uses your first name too soon and too often, talks about 'the future of this town', and states every sum to the dollar.
npcs.goal: Get the new bridge built downstream on Sturdivant bottomland, sell the state the right-of-way and own the truck stop at the new interchange.
npcs.secret: He is two years behind on the family's timber loans, and he has asked Dr. Phillip Sayle in Calder to find his mother Vada unfit so he can sign the bottomland over himself.
npcs.history: Carter Sturdivant grew up in Sturdivant House, went to college in Calder and came home in 2014 to run the business when his father died in the timber woods. He lives with his mother and drives a new truck every two years. Half the notes and leases in town are in his company's name.

npcs.name: Jolene Overstreet
npcs.role: mayor and town clerk
npcs.look: Heavy-set woman in her fifties in a cardigan over a church T-shirt, with a lanyard of keys and a phone she keeps checking for a signal it never finds.
npcs.voice: Brisk and procedural; cites ordinances by number, says 'that's a council matter' to shut a subject, and drops to a whisper to say anything kind.
npcs.goal: Get the downstream bridge approved and the police department dissolved before the town's money runs out in January.
npcs.secret: Carter Sturdivant pays her five hundred dollars a month in cash, handed over in the motel parking lot, and she used the first year of it to cover money missing from the water fund.
npcs.history: Jolene Overstreet has been town clerk since 1998 and mayor since 2018, the year nobody else filed. She married Gerald in 1991, and they raised Annette in the yellow house behind Town Hall. She runs the council by the book and the town's money with a calculator and a prayer.

memories.text: Loose end with Tester (a debt): I owe a man in this town six hundred dollars I don't have.
Tester let the six hundred go past due, so I took the phone as a start.
Tester let the six hundred go past due, so I took the phone as a start.

npcs.name: Hollis Byrd
npcs.role: owner of Byrd's Pawn and a member of the town council
npcs.look: Stooped, pot-bellied man of sixty-five in suspenders and a fishing vest, with a jeweler's loupe on a cord and a toothpick that never leaves his mouth.
npcs.voice: Slow and sideways, never a straight yes or no; calls everything 'merchandise', prices things before you ask, and says 'I don't ask where, I ask how much.'
npcs.goal: Sell the shop and retire to the coast before the bridge closes and the building is worth nothing.
npcs.secret: He runs the Night Run's cash through his books as pawn sales, and the catalytic converters stacked behind the shop came off cars in three counties.

whenTold.memory: was told Hollis Byrd runs the landing's cash through his pawn books
whenTold.inquiry: Chief Bell spends a morning at Byrd's Pawn going through the ledgers.
whenTold.news: Chief Bell spent a morning at Byrd's Pawn going through the ledgers.

npcs.history: Hollis Byrd has run the pawn shop on Front Street since 1988, raised his daughter Renee on his own in the apartment over it and has sat on the town council since 2002. He fishes off the landing at night and knows the price of everything in three counties. He has not spoken to Renee since 2023, and she did not ask him to her wedding.

npcs.name: Wade Purvis
npcs.role: owner of Purvis Landing and boss of the Night Run
npcs.look: Lean, sunburnt man in his fifties with a gray ponytail, a faded camouflage cap and the tip of one finger missing.
npcs.voice: Quiet and dry; lets you talk yourself out, answers in river terms like stage, chop and slack water, and never says the word police, only 'the law'.
npcs.goal: Keep the old bridge open and the river unwatched after dark, and keep his nephew out of prison.
npcs.secret: He knows Colt is selling pills on the side and has not stopped him, because Colt was there the night Wade beat Calvin Ogletree half to death below the landing for cutting in on the run, and could send him to prison for it.

whenTold.memory: was told Wade Purvis beat Calvin Ogletree half to death below the landing
whenTold.inquiry: Chief Bell drives to the county home in Clayburn to see Calvin Ogletree.
whenTold.news: Chief Bell drove to Clayburn to see Calvin Ogletree in the county home.

npcs.history: Wade Purvis grew up at the landing and has run it since 1989, with Lorna beside him since they married in 1993. His younger brother Dale is in the state penitentiary, and Wade has looked out for Dale's boy Colt since he was fourteen. He drinks one beer at the Low Water every evening and is back at the landing by dark.

npcs.name: Colt Purvis
npcs.role: deckhand on the Night Run
npcs.look: Wiry kid of twenty-two in a sleeveless shirt and white rubber boots, with a fresh tattoo still peeling on his forearm.
npcs.voice: Fast and jumpy; talks over you, calls men 'bro' and women 'ma'am', brags about money he doesn't have, and laughs at things that aren't funny.
npcs.goal: Make enough money to quit working for his uncle and buy a truck in his own name.
npcs.secret: He sells pain pills bought across the river to people at Riverbend, and the bottle Amber Lott died with came from him.

whenTold.memory: was told Colt Purvis sold Amber Lott the pills
whenTold.inquiry: Chief Bell starts asking at Riverbend who sells pills to kids.
whenTold.news: Chief Bell has been asking at Riverbend who sells pills to kids.

npcs.history: Colt Purvis was fourteen when his father Dale went to the state penitentiary, and he grew up between his uncle's landing and a trailer at Riverbend. He quit school at sixteen to work the boats for Wade. He gets a new tattoo every few months and talks about the truck he is going to buy.

npcs.name: Marcus Bell
npcs.role: chief of police
npcs.look: Tall, heavy-shouldered man of fifty in a pressed uniform shirt gone tight at the buttons, with a shaved head and a limp he hides badly.
npcs.voice: Courteous and relentless; says 'sir' and 'ma'am', asks the same question three different ways, and writes your answers in a pocket notebook while you watch him do it.
npcs.goal: Make a bust big enough to save his department before the council votes to dissolve it, and prove the bridge report was bought.
npcs.secret: He has known for months that Travis Cagle takes Night Run money and has let it go on, because he needs Travis on the payroll until the vote and on the witness stand after it.
npcs.history: Marcus Bell left the Calder police for the chief's job in Lockett's Ferry in 2010, after a knee injury ended his patrol days. He lives in a room behind the station and calls his sister Celeste every Sunday night. The council has tried to cut his budget every year he has been here.

npcs.name: Travis Cagle
npcs.role: night-shift police officer
npcs.look: Thick-necked man of twenty-eight in a uniform with the sleeves rolled, a dip of tobacco in his lip and a new watch too nice for his pay.
npcs.voice: Loud and buddy-buddy, all 'my man' and 'hoss'; talks about his boat, laughs before his own punchlines, and goes quiet the second anyone mentions money.
npcs.goal: Keep taking Wade Purvis's money until his boat is paid off, then get on with the county before anyone looks closely.
npcs.secret: Wade Purvis pays him three hundred dollars a week to park at the motel during the runs, and he keeps Wade's texts on a second phone in case he ever needs to trade them.
npcs.history: Travis Cagle grew up at Riverbend, played linebacker at the county school and joined the town police in 2019. He works nights, lives with Shayla Rawls in her trailer and spends his days off on the river in his bass boat.

npcs.name: Ray Dees
npcs.role: pastor of Riverside Baptist Church
npcs.look: Round-faced man of sixty-five in a short-sleeved white shirt and clip-on tie, with a hearing aid and a pocket full of peppermints.
npcs.voice: Slow and warm, with a preacher's rhythm even at the gas pump; sometimes answers a hard question with a Bible story, and somehow gets the answer out of you instead.
npcs.goal: Keep the Riverbend families housed and fed through the winter, and bury no more young people this year.
npcs.secret: The church's new roof was paid for by an anonymous cash gift that he knows came from Wade Purvis, and he has preached against the Night Run every Sunday since without giving a dollar of it back.
npcs.history: Ray Dees has been pastor of Riverside Baptist since 1994 and has married, baptized or buried most of the town. He and Nadine raised their daughter Leah in the Parsonage, and now they are raising her son Micah while she is in treatment in Calder. He drives a trunk full of groceries out to Riverbend every afternoon.

npcs.name: June Satterfield
npcs.role: retired nurse who patches people up at her kitchen table
npcs.look: Stout woman of sixty in scrub pants and a sweatshirt from a hospital that closed, with her gray hair in a clip and a canvas bag that rattles.
npcs.voice: Blunt and clinical; asks what you took and how much before she asks your name, swears mildly, and never tells anyone not to worry.
npcs.goal: Keep Riverbend's people out of an emergency room forty miles away, and get the pills off the lot without anyone she knows going to prison.
npcs.secret: She has reversed four overdoses at Riverbend this fall without reporting one, and three of the four told her they bought from Colt Purvis.
npcs.history: June Satterfield was a nurse at the old county hospital in Clayburn for twenty-six years, until it closed in 2019. She and Burl have lived at Riverbend since, and her kitchen table is where Riverbend goes for stitches, blood pressure and bad news. She keeps a bag of supplies by the door.

npcs.name: Dewayne Mangum
npcs.role: mechanic in the service bays at Pittman's
npcs.look: Short, broad man of forty with grease worked into every knuckle, safety glasses pushed up on a bald head and a shop rag in his back pocket.
npcs.voice: Few words, all of them about engines; says 'mm-hm' for yes and 'well' for no, and talks to the truck he's working on more than to you.
npcs.goal: Save enough to buy the empty garage on Front Street and stop working out of Royce Pittman's bays.
npcs.secret: On the morning of the bridge inspection he towed the engineer's rental car out of a ditch and watched Carter Sturdivant drive the man off to lunch, though the report says he spent the whole day under the spans.
npcs.history: Dewayne Mangum learned engines under Wiley Tackett on Front Street and has worked the service bays at Pittman's since 2012. He married Mavis in 2008, and they moved into her mother Inez's house up the river road in 2021 to look after her. He fishes at Purvis Landing most evenings and says about ten words a day.

memories.text: Loose end with Tester (a secret): Someone here knows what I did before I came.

npcs.name: Tyler Rasberry
npcs.role: night clerk at the Riverview Motor Court
npcs.look: Gangly young man of nineteen with a patchy beard, a gaming headset round his neck and a phone with a cracked screen always in his hand.
npcs.voice: Mumbles and deflects with internet jokes and never meets your eye, then turns precise the moment cash is on the counter: plates, times, room numbers.
npcs.goal: Save enough cash to leave Lockett's Ferry for good and never work another night shift.
npcs.secret: The motel's parking-lot camera has caught Carter Sturdivant handing Jolene Overstreet an envelope every month since spring, and Tyler has copied the clips to a thumb drive he is trying to sell.
npcs.history: Tyler Rasberry finished at the county school in May and took the night desk at the motor court because it was the only job going. He shares a trailer at Riverbend with his cousin Brianna, who cleans the rooms he rents out, and plays games online on the motel wifi until dawn.

npcs.name: Tammy Lott
npcs.role: cook at the Low Water
npcs.look: Hollow-eyed woman of forty-two in a hairnet and a stained Low Water T-shirt, with her daughter's name tattooed fresh on the inside of her wrist.
npcs.voice: Hoarse and short; says exactly what she thinks in as few words as possible, swears at the grill, and goes very calm and polite when she is angriest.
npcs.goal: See whoever sold Amber the pills that killed her locked up or run out of town.
npcs.secret: She took a tire iron to Colt Purvis's truck the week after the funeral, and Wade Purvis paid for the windshield himself and told her the next one would cost her more.
npcs.history: Tammy Lott has cooked at the Low Water since 2010 and raised Amber and Austin on her own in the Lott Trailer. Since Amber died in August she has worked every shift Loretta will give her. She put up the cross by the Riverbend mailboxes and the sign in her front window.

npcs.name: Mavis Mangum
npcs.role: night manager at the Riverview Motor Court
npcs.look: Small, sharp-faced woman of forty-one with dyed black hair scraped into a clip, a motel key ring on a coiled cord around her wrist and an unlit cigarette behind one ear.
npcs.voice: Clipped and sour; tells you what a thing will cost her before she says yes or no, calls people mister or miss like a complaint, and jingles her keys when she wants you gone.
npcs.goal: Keep the motor court open and her job with it, which means keeping the old bridge, and talk Dewayne out of the Front Street garage.
npcs.secret: In the spring she emptied the account Dewayne was saving for the garage to pay off a note Sturdivant Land and Timber held on her late mother's house, and she has been putting it back out of the motel till one cash room at a time.
npcs.history: Mavis Mangum, born Mavis Crocker, grew up in the white frame house up the river road and has run the motor court's night desk since 2016. She married Dewayne in 2008, came home in 2021 to care for her mother Inez and kept the house when Inez died. She answers to Stanley Wexler by email and to nobody in person.

npcs.name: Darlene Pittman
npcs.role: Royce's wife, who keeps the books at Pittman's
npcs.look: Tall, careful woman in her fifties with a short silver bob, a blouse buttoned to the collar and a pencil she taps against her teeth while she adds.
npcs.voice: Polite and exact; answers questions about Royce with figures instead of feelings, slips into talking about him in the past tense, and excuses herself to get back to the books.
npcs.goal: Keep the station and the house out of Carter Sturdivant's hands, however Royce votes.
npcs.secret: She has known about Royce and Loretta Gaddis for years and keeps a folder of dates and photographs in the station safe, to use the day Royce tries to sign anything without her.
npcs.history: Darlene Pittman grew up in Clayburn, married Royce in 1996 and has kept the station's books ever since. She runs the church flower committee, never misses one of Kaylee's games and is the one in the family who reads the fine print.

npcs.name: Kaylee Pittman
npcs.role: Royce's daughter, who works the register after school
npcs.look: Sixteen-year-old girl with a long brown ponytail, a softball team hoodie and nails painted the green of the station sign.
npcs.voice: Deadpan; answers in as few words as she can get away with, then says out loud the one thing about you nobody else noticed.
npcs.goal: Win a softball scholarship and get out of town before her parents stop pretending.
npcs.secret: She drives her father's truck up to the water tower at night for signal, and she has seen Travis Cagle's patrol car parked dark behind the motor court every night the boats go across.
npcs.history: Kaylee Pittman is a junior at the county school and the starting pitcher on its softball team. She works the register at the station after school and on weekends. Her grandfather Clyde's photo over the register is the one thing at the station she will not let anyone move.

awayOn.where: at the county school in Clayburn

npcs.name: Nadine Dees
npcs.role: church secretary and pianist at Riverside Baptist
npcs.look: Plump, bright-eyed woman of sixty-three in a holiday sweater whatever the season, with reading glasses pushed up into her curls.
npcs.voice: Chirpy and thorough; reads records aloud in full, including the parts you did not ask for, and says bless you when she means go away.
npcs.goal: Keep the church records straight and the fellowship hall pantry stocked through the winter.
npcs.secret: For forty dollars a time she has changed names and dates in the baptism and membership books for people who needed a different past, and the torn-out pages, the oldest one torn out for her own daughter Leah, are in a shoebox in the parsonage closet that Ray has never opened.
npcs.history: Nadine Dees has been church secretary and pianist at Riverside Baptist since 1994. She keeps the baptism and membership books, runs the pantry in the fellowship hall and knows everybody's birthday. Since July she has been raising her grandson Micah while her daughter Leah is in treatment.

npcs.name: Micah Dees
npcs.role: Ray's grandson, who works the Purvis Landing bait shop
npcs.look: Lanky seventeen-year-old boy with a grown-out buzz cut, a church camp T-shirt and fish scales dried on his jeans.
npcs.voice: Says yes ma'am and no sir on reflex, then mumbles the true answer right after, as if he hopes you missed it.
npcs.goal: Pay for another month of his mother's treatment program in the city without his grandparents finding out where the money comes from.
npcs.secret: Wade Purvis pays him fifty dollars a night to sit in the dark bait shop and flash the dock light twice when a patrol car comes down the river road.
npcs.history: Micah Dees moved into the Parsonage with his grandparents in July, when his mother Leah went into the Willows in Calder. He is a senior at the county school and works the bait shop at Purvis Landing for Lorna Purvis. He goes to see his mother every Sunday his grandfather can drive him.

awayOn.where: at the county school in Clayburn

npcs.name: Austin Lott
npcs.role: Tammy's son, Amber Lott's little brother
npcs.look: Skinny fifteen-year-old boy in a hand-me-down Army jacket, with a bike he never locks and his sister's name written on his sneakers in marker.
npcs.voice: Says almost nothing to grown-ups, then asks one question too exact for his age, like what time somebody's truck usually leaves.
npcs.goal: Prove that Colt Purvis sold Amber the pills and put the proof in front of someone who will act on it.
npcs.secret: He has followed Colt on his bike for weeks and knows about the tackle box on the girder under the first span of the old bridge, but he will not tell anyone until he can hand it to the state police himself.
npcs.history: Austin Lott is a freshman at the county school when he goes, and rides his bike everywhere else. Since his sister Amber died in August he has stopped talking to most grown-ups. Annette Overstreet is the one teacher who still gets an answer out of him.

awayOn.where: at the county school in Clayburn

npcs.name: Odessa Fairley
npcs.role: housekeeper and companion to Vada Sturdivant
npcs.look: Tall, gray-haired woman of sixty-six in a starched apron over a church dress, with a small silver cross at her throat and shoes that make no sound.
npcs.voice: Soft and exact; says Miss Vada says when she means herself, and hums a hymn under her breath when she disapproves of what you just said.
npcs.goal: Keep Miss Vada in her own house to the end, the way she promised her.
npcs.secret: Carter has offered her five thousand dollars to tell Dr. Sayle that Vada wanders at night and leaves the stove on, and she has not said no yet, because Sturdivant Land and Timber holds the note on her sister's house.
npcs.history: Odessa Fairley grew up in Clayburn and has kept house for Vada Sturdivant since 1979, the year Amos Sturdivant died. She lives in the back bedroom of Sturdivant House, sings in the choir at Riverside Baptist and drives to see her sister Corinne on her Sunday afternoons off.

npcs.name: Lyman Coker
npcs.role: night bartender at the Low Water
npcs.look: Gaunt man of seventy in a pearl-snap shirt, with an oxygen tube looped over his ears and a ledger of bar tabs in his shirt pocket.
npcs.voice: Gloomy and courteous; expects the worst of everyone and thanks you, sincerely, when you prove him right.
npcs.goal: Keep his regulars paid up and out of trouble, and keep the job long enough to never see the county home.
npcs.secret: He reads every letter and package anyone leaves with him before he hands it over, and he has steamed open two envelopes Carter Sturdivant left at the bar for Jolene Overstreet.
npcs.history: Lyman Coker drove a log truck for thirty years until his lungs gave out, and has tended bar nights at the Low Water since 2015. He rents a room by the week at the motor court and plays cribbage with Curtis Pruett between customers.

memories.text: kept quiet about what I told them and stood up for me

npcs.name: Elbert Gentry
npcs.role: the oldest man in town and on the town council, whose granddaddy ran the last ferry
npcs.look: Bent, bright-eyed man of eighty-eight in suspenders and a cap from the 1982 bass tournament, with a cane carved from a cypress knee.
npcs.voice: Tells you the year of everything, and corrects other people's stories about the river with the date it really happened and who drowned.
npcs.goal: See the old bridge stand until he is buried, because his granddaddy lost the ferry to it and made his peace.
npcs.secret: As a boy after the war he rowed whiskey across the river for Amos Sturdivant, and the Gentry family Bible on his nightstand holds a page in his granddaddy Asa's hand naming who Amos paid at the state highway department in 1938.
npcs.history: Elbert Gentry was born in the Gentry House in 1938, the year the bridge opened and his granddaddy Asa's ferry closed. He worked at the paper mill for forty years, has sat on the town council since 1983 and spends his mornings on the Front Street bench and his afternoons at the Low Water. His sister Pearl and his granddaughter Glenda live with him.

npcs.name: Pearl Gentry
npcs.role: columnist for the county weekly
npcs.look: Tiny woman of seventy-nine in a lavender pantsuit, with a steno pad in her purse and a pencil stuck through her white bun.
npcs.voice: Talks in newspaper headlines, asks for the spelling of your name before she asks anything else, and writes your answers down whether you like it or not.
npcs.goal: Write the true story of the bridge vote before somebody from the city writes a wrong one.
npcs.secret: She has kept every birth, marriage and death notice the town printed in fifty years, with the ones families paid her to leave out, and one of those is about Carter Sturdivant.
npcs.history: Pearl Gentry has written the Lockett's Ferry column in the county weekly since 1975: births, deaths, church news and who had company. She clerked at the courthouse in Clayburn for thirty years and moved back into the Gentry House with her brother Elbert when she retired. She walks down to Town Hall every afternoon to read the council papers.

npcs.name: Glenda Pryor
npcs.role: police dispatcher and clerk at Town Hall
npcs.look: Broad, freckled woman of forty with a dispatch headset pushed back in her red hair and a cardigan pocket full of pens.
npcs.voice: Talks in radio shorthand out of habit, ten-four and what is your twenty, and repeats the last thing you said back to you as a question.
npcs.goal: Keep her job, and her grandfather's medicine paid for, when the council votes on the police.
npcs.secret: She tapes every call that comes into the station on a cassette recorder under the desk, including the one that warned Wade Purvis's people the chief was on his way to the ramp.
npcs.history: Glenda Pryor grew up in the Gentry House with her grandfather Elbert and has dispatched for the town police since 2007. She knows every voice that calls the station and most of what they want. She keeps Elbert's medicines straight and drives him to his appointments in Calder.

npcs.name: Nikki Ballard
npcs.role: day-shift police officer
npcs.look: Compact, sunburned woman of thirty-one with a tight braid, a vest one size too big and mirrored sunglasses she takes off to look at you.
npcs.voice: Brisk and dry; asks for your ID before small talk, answers a joke with the single word noted, and never fills a silence.
npcs.goal: Keep a badge when the department dissolves, here or with the county.
npcs.secret: She has already interviewed with the county sheriff and promised to bring him Chief Bell's case files if the council votes the department out.
npcs.history: Nikki Ballard came from the police academy two years ago and is the department's only day officer. She rents the apartment over Byrd's Pawn from Hollis Byrd, runs five miles on the river road every morning and keeps to herself.

npcs.name: Virgil Odom
npcs.role: retired state bridge inspector who fishes the pier
npcs.look: Lean, stooped man of seventy-two in a faded state highway cap, with a rusty tape measure clipped to his belt and a bucket of cut bait.
npcs.voice: Speaks in load ratings and rust, ends an opinion with that is not my opinion, that is steel, and taps whatever he leans on to listen to it.
npcs.goal: Get someone to read his own inspection reports before the state tears down a bridge he says is good for twenty more years.
npcs.secret: Warren Pettit, the engineer the state sent, called him the week before the inspection to ask what the bridge would need to fail, and Virgil told him, and has been ashamed of it every day since.
leverageKeys: what it would need to fail
npcs.history: Virgil Odom inspected bridges for the state highway department for thirty-four years and inspected the old bridge eleven times. His daughter Ruth died three winters ago, and he moved out to the Haskins Farm with Lamar and Trent the next spring. He fishes off the pier under the first span most afternoons.

npcs.name: Annette Overstreet
npcs.role: seventh-grade teacher at the county middle school
npcs.look: Slight woman of thirty-four with short dark hair, chalk dust on one sleeve and a tote bag of ungraded papers she carries everywhere.
npcs.voice: Patient and precise; explains things in numbered steps whether you asked or not, and checks with make sense? before she lets you go.
npcs.goal: Keep Austin Lott in school through the spring, and keep Micah Dees from quitting before he graduates.
npcs.secret: She is the one who called the state about the bridge, after a loaded log truck passed her on the first span and she felt the deck drop under her car, and she has never told anyone in town, least of all Jolene.
npcs.history: Annette Overstreet teaches seventh grade at the county school in Clayburn and came home to the yellow house in 2022 after six years teaching in Calder. She tutors Austin Lott and Micah Dees at the church on Wednesday nights. She and her mother disagree about almost everything.

awayOn.where: at the county school in Clayburn

npcs.name: Gerald Overstreet
npcs.role: Jolene's husband, retired from the paper mill
npcs.look: Big, slow man of sixty-one in house slippers and a mill union jacket, with a police scanner clipped to his belt and turned up loud.
npcs.voice: Starts half of what he says with scanner says, repeats every call he heard that day, and calls his wife the mayor even at supper.
npcs.goal: Get Jolene to quit before whatever she is mixed up in comes out.
npcs.secret: He found Jolene's envelope of cash in the chest freezer last spring, counted it and put it back, and he has written down every date it got fatter.
npcs.history: Gerald Overstreet ran the paper machines at the mill for thirty-three years until it closed in 2016. He married Jolene in 1991, keeps the house and the scanner going and repeats the day's calls at supper. He has not been much past the end of the drive since his knees went.

npcs.name: Lamar Haskins
npcs.role: farmer and council member who leases Sturdivant land
npcs.look: Thick, weathered man of fifty-eight in a seed company cap and mud-caked boots, with a farmer's tan that stops at his sleeves.
npcs.voice: Slow and careful; talks in acres, bushels and inches of rain, and checks the sky before he answers anything hard.
npcs.goal: Get the downstream bridge built across the fields he leases, because Carter promised him a buyout that would clear his equipment loans.
npcs.secret: He has already signed Carter's option papers on the lease, which he had no right to do while Vada is alive, and the check is sitting uncashed in his glove box.
npcs.history: Lamar Haskins has farmed the family land and the leased Sturdivant bottomland since he was twenty, and has sat on the town council for eight years. His wife Ruth died three winters ago, and he lives at the farm with their son Trent and Ruth's father Virgil.

npcs.name: Trent Haskins
npcs.role: Lamar's son, who drives the farm's grain truck
npcs.look: Broad, easygoing man of twenty-four in a sleeveless camo shirt and a feed-store cap turned backward, with a sunburned neck and a cooler always in reach.
npcs.voice: Easy and friendly; calls everybody cuz, is always halfway out the door on some errand, and laughs off a question with gotta run.
npcs.goal: Keep his father and his grandfather from finding out what the grain truck carries at night.
npcs.secret: Twice a week he drives cases of liquor across the old bridge in the grain truck for Wade Purvis, a hundred pounds under the limit, and his own father's bridge vote would put him out of that work.
npcs.history: Trent Haskins drives the farm's grain truck and does whatever hauling anyone will pay for. He was two years ahead of Colt Purvis at the county school and has been his best friend since. His mother Ruth's death hit him hardest of the three men at the farm.

npcs.name: Leon Varner
npcs.role: repo man who buys bad debts for a title-loan outfit
npcs.look: Heavy man of forty-seven in a golf shirt and wraparound sunglasses, with a clipboard under one arm and a tow truck he never turns off.
npcs.voice: Polite and slow; calls you friend and works the late fees into every other sentence, the way another man would mention the weather.
npcs.goal: Clear his list of overdue accounts in the county before the month is out, with fees.
npcs.secret: He bought most of the debts on his list for a dime on the dollar from the lender Carter Sturdivant uses, and he would settle any of them for half if somebody pushed.
npcs.history: Leon Varner has repossessed trucks and collected bad debts in the south end of the county for six years, for Wendell Strunk's title-loan office in Clayburn. He rents a room by the week at the motor court while he works through his list, and nobody is glad to see his tow truck.

npcs.name: Curtis Pruett
npcs.role: insurance man who runs the card game at the Low Water
npcs.look: Dapper man of fifty-two in a short-sleeved dress shirt and a bolo tie, with a pinky ring and a deck of cards he shuffles one-handed.
npcs.voice: Puts odds on everything, offers to settle any argument with a bet, and never says a number without saying what it pays.
npcs.goal: Win back the house his wife put him out of, one Friday game at a time.
npcs.secret: He takes bets on the bridge vote from both sides, and Royce Pittman owes him eleven hundred dollars he lost on the game in October.
npcs.history: Curtis Pruett sells insurance out of his truck across three counties and has run the card game at the Low Water for fifteen years. His wife Lynette put him out of their house in Clayburn last winter, and he has had a room at the motor court since.

memories.text: Loose end with Tester (an enemy): Someone I wronged is already here, waiting for me.

npcs.name: Boyd Teague
npcs.role: stranger who has had Room 9 at the motor court a week
npcs.look: Big, quiet man of fifty in a pressed denim shirt, with a healed scar through one eyebrow and knuckles like walnuts.
npcs.voice: Says very little, all of it polite, and always uses a person's full name, first and last, as if he were reading it off a list.
npcs.goal: Settle an old account with someone in Lockett's Ferry, quietly, and be gone before the law notices him.
npcs.secret: He left his parole two states over without permission, so one phone call would send him back; he came for Wade Purvis, who gave his name to the law in 2018 to keep his own out of Dale's case, and Wade's is the first name on his list.
npcs.history: Boyd Teague checked into Room 9 at the motor court a week ago and paid two weeks in cash. Nobody in town knows where he came from or what he wants, and he has not said. He keeps to his room in the mornings and walks out on the old bridge every afternoon to look down at the landing.

npcs.name: Jodie Strayhorn
npcs.role: new waitress at the Low Water
npcs.look: Wiry woman of twenty-nine with bleached hair growing out dark, a Low Water apron and a fading bruise she covers with makeup.
npcs.voice: Quick and bright with the customers, then flat and careful the second anyone asks where she is from, and she changes the subject to the specials.
npcs.goal: Find out who beat her uncle half to death below the landing, and leave before anyone learns her real name.
npcs.secret: Her real name is Jodie Ogletree: she is Bernice Ogletree's daughter, she skipped bail in the next state over, and she took the job at the Low Water to find out who beat her uncle Calvin below the landing.
npcs.history: Jodie Strayhorn turned up at the Low Water three weeks ago asking for work, and Loretta hired her that night. She sleeps in the back room of the bar, works every shift she can get and says she is from up north when anyone asks.

npcs.name: Lorna Purvis
npcs.role: Wade's wife, who runs the bait shop at Purvis Landing
npcs.look: Round, cheerful woman of fifty-five in rubber clogs, with a fishing-lure earring in one ear and a tub of crickets on the counter beside her.
npcs.voice: Bait-shop chatter about what is biting and where, and the moment you ask about Wade, a bright you would have to ask him.
npcs.goal: Keep the landing, the shop and her husband out of court until they can sell up and go.
npcs.secret: Calvin Ogletree, the man Wade beat half to death for cutting in on the run, is alive in the county home in Clayburn, and she sends his sister Bernice two hundred dollars every month out of the bait shop till.
npcs.history: Lorna Purvis married Wade in 1993 and has run the bait shop at the landing ever since. She knows what is biting, who caught it and who is lying about it. She has fed her nephew Colt since his father Dale went away, and pays Micah Dees to help in the shop.

npcs.name: Brianna Tolliver
npcs.role: housekeeper at the Riverview Motor Court
npcs.look: Pale, thin young woman of twenty-three in a motel smock, with chipped nail polish and a hospital bracelet she has not cut off.
npcs.voice: Soft and quick; apologizes before she says anything, sorry, sorry, and says thank you twice for anything at all.
npcs.goal: Stay clean, keep the job and save enough for a used car that runs.
npcs.secret: She is one of the four people June Satterfield brought back from an overdose this fall, and she still owes Colt Purvis forty dollars for the pills.
npcs.history: Brianna Tolliver grew up at Riverbend with her cousin Tyler, shares a trailer there with him and has cleaned rooms at the motor court since the spring. She is saving for a car and walks to work along the highway in the meantime.

npcs.name: Shayla Rawls
npcs.role: hairdresser who works out of her trailer at Riverbend
npcs.look: Pretty, round-faced woman of twenty-five in a hairdresser's smock, with a vape pen in one hand and two phones in the other.
npcs.voice: Sweet and sticky; calls you sugar and asks three personal questions for every one you answer.
npcs.goal: Turn what she hears in her chair into enough cash to open a real salon at the county seat.
npcs.secret: She found Travis's second phone and photographed every text on it, and she is deciding whether to sell the pictures to Chief Bell or to Wade Purvis.
npcs.history: Shayla Rawls went to beauty school in Calder and came back to do hair out of her trailer at Riverbend for fifteen dollars a cut. Travis Cagle has lived with her since last year, and half the town's news passes through her chair.

npcs.name: Dwight Spann
npcs.role: timber foreman for Sturdivant Land and Timber
npcs.look: Rangy man of forty-nine in a hi-vis vest over a flannel shirt, with a can of survey paint in his hand and sunflower-seed shells on his boots.
npcs.voice: Few words and a lot of spat sunflower seeds; never says Carter, only Mr. Sturdivant, and answers anything else with that is above my pay.
npcs.goal: Keep his crew working through the winter by doing whatever Mr. Sturdivant asks.
npcs.secret: On Carter's orders he moved the survey stakes for the downstream bridge off the Haskins forty and onto the Sturdivant bottomland the night before the state crew came, so the state would have to buy its right-of-way from the Sturdivants.
npcs.history: Dwight Spann has run a Sturdivant Land and Timber crew in the pine upriver for eighteen years, since Harlan Voss hired him. He lives alone in a trailer at Riverbend and goes up to Sturdivant House every morning for his orders.

memories.text: helped carry the outboard motor down to the ramp

npcs.name: Burl Satterfield
npcs.role: June's husband, who fixes outboard motors
npcs.look: Wide, red-faced man of sixty-six in bib overalls, with a lineman's scarred hands and a bent outboard propeller he files smooth while he talks.
npcs.voice: Talks too loud after forty years around power lines, says what's that? and then answers what he thought you said.
npcs.goal: Keep June from wearing herself out on everybody at Riverbend.
npcs.secret: He rebuilt the motors on two of Wade Purvis's johnboats this fall for cash and told June the money came from his pension.
npcs.history: Burl Satterfield climbed power poles for the co-op for forty years and retired in 2019 with a pension and bad hearing. He and June moved to Riverbend that year, and he fixes outboard motors for anyone at the landing who brings him one. Wiley Tackett was his best friend.

npcs.name: Amber Lott
npcs.role: Tammy's daughter, who died at nineteen
npcs.look: Remembered as a freckled girl of nineteen with a pink streak dyed in her hair, a nose ring and a laugh you could hear from the far end of the Riverbend loop.
npcs.voice: Talked fast and loud and called everybody by a nickname she had made up for them, and her mother still uses a few of them without meaning to.
npcs.goal: Wanted to finish a nursing assistant course in Clayburn and get herself and her brother out of Riverbend.
npcs.secret: She had been clean for two months when she died, and the pills that killed her were the first she had bought since telling June Satterfield she was done with them.
npcs.history: Amber grew up in the Lott Trailer and worked a drive-through window in Clayburn after she quit school. She died at Riverbend in August, at nineteen, and is buried in Riverside Cemetery under a funeral-home marker until there is money for a stone.

npcs.name: Ruth Haskins
npcs.role: Lamar's late wife and Virgil's daughter
npcs.look: Remembered as a tall, sunburned woman of forty-seven in a seed company cap, who drove the grain truck herself at harvest.
npcs.voice: Laughed at her own jokes before she got to the end of them, and said well, bless it whenever anything broke on the farm.
npcs.goal: Wanted to see the farm paid off and Trent settled before she was fifty.
npcs.secret: The year before she died she told her father the farm was two seasons from losing its equipment, and made him promise never to let Lamar sell out to the Sturdivants.
npcs.history: Ruth was Virgil Odom's only daughter and married Lamar Haskins at twenty-two. She kept the farm's books, drove the grain truck at harvest and taught Sunday school at Riverside Baptist until the cancer. She died three winters ago, and her father moved out to the farm the spring after.

npcs.name: Amos Sturdivant
npcs.role: Vada's father, who fought the state for the bridge in 1938
npcs.look: Known from one photograph in Town Hall: a lean man in a white suit at the bridge ribbon-cutting in 1938, hat in hand and squinting at the camera.
npcs.voice: Said to have talked like a preacher and bargained like a horse trader, and never to have written down a promise he could make out loud.
npcs.goal: Wanted a bridge at Lockett's Ferry with the Sturdivant name on the plaque, and got both.
npcs.secret: He ran whiskey into the dry county from the 1920s into the 1950s, the last years with Elbert Gentry rowing it, and the cash he paid the state highway department in 1938 is why the bridge was built here and not somewhere else.
npcs.history: Amos Sturdivant bought the bottomland and the hill in the 1920s and built Sturdivant House. He spent three years fighting the state for a bridge and stood on it the day it opened in 1938. His name is on the plaque at the town end of the old bridge.

npcs.name: Harlan Voss
npcs.died: October 2014, a heart attack in the timber woods
npcs.role: Vada's late husband and Carter's father, who ran the timber side of the business
npcs.look: Remembered as a heavy, red-faced man of seventy-one in khaki work clothes and a straw hat, with a tally book in his shirt pocket and mud to the knees.
npcs.voice: Talked timber prices to anyone who would listen, called every man buddy, and could not tell a story without starting it in the woods.
npcs.goal: Wanted Sturdivant Land and Timber to outlast him with Carter at the head of it.
npcs.secret: In his last years he borrowed against the timber from Garland Teasley without telling Vada, and the loans Carter is behind on now are his.
npcs.history: Harlan Voss came from upriver to buy timber, married Vada Sturdivant in 1977 and ran the timber side of the business for thirty years. Vada kept her name, and their son carries it. He died in the timber woods in 2014 and is buried beside her father.

npcs.name: Inez Crocker
npcs.role: Mavis's late mother, whose house the Mangums live in
npcs.look: Remembered as a small, sharp woman of sixty-nine in a quilted housecoat, with a church fan in one hand and the TV remote in the other.
npcs.voice: Told everybody exactly what she thought of them, to their face, and called it being honest.
npcs.goal: Wanted to die in her own house, owing nobody, with Mavis there.
npcs.secret: She signed a contract for deed with Sturdivant Land and Timber on the house in 2016 to pay her hospital bills, and Mavis never knew until the papers came after the funeral.
npcs.history: Inez Crocker lived in the white frame house up the river road for forty years and worked in the office at the paper mill until it closed. Mavis and Dewayne moved in to look after her in 2021. She died in that house in February of last year.

npcs.name: Asa Gentry
npcs.role: Elbert's granddaddy, who ran the last ferry
npcs.look: Known from the photographs in the Gentry House: a bent, white-bearded man in a slouch hat, standing at the ferry's sweep with the river high behind him.
npcs.voice: Said to have answered every question with the river's height that morning, and to have charged strangers double and widows nothing.
npcs.goal: Wanted the ferry to last as long as he did, and it nearly did.
npcs.secret: He took Amos Sturdivant's money to stop fighting the bridge in 1937, and the Gentrys have called it a fair price ever since.
npcs.history: Asa Gentry ran the Gentry ferry across the Lusk for fifty years, until the bridge opened in 1938 and the ferry was cut loose. He built the Gentry House, sat on its porch watching the bridge traffic for thirteen more years and died in the winter of 1951.

npcs.name: Wiley Tackett
npcs.role: the mechanic who ran the garage on Front Street for forty-five years
npcs.look: Remembered as a short, bowlegged man of seventy-seven in a work shirt with his name over the pocket, never without a cigarette.
npcs.voice: Talked to engines like they were mules, cussed them the same, and taught half the boys in town to change their own oil.
npcs.goal: Wanted Dewayne Mangum to have the garage when he was gone.
npcs.secret: He told Burl Satterfield he had left the garage to Dewayne, but the Sturdivants held the note on the building, and the will he left gave it back to them.
npcs.history: Wiley Tackett fixed cars in the garage on Front Street from 1979 until he got too sick to stand. Dewayne Mangum learned the trade under him before he went to work for Royce Pittman. The bay doors have been chained since he died, three springs ago.

npcs.name: Clyde Pittman
npcs.died: summer of 2009, a heart attack at the pumps
npcs.role: Royce's late daddy, who opened Pittman's in 1966
npcs.look: Remembered as a big, bald man of sixty-nine in a white station shirt, with a cigar he never lit and a ring of keys on his belt.
npcs.voice: Told the same six stories at the register for forty years, and Royce tells them now, word for word, as if they happened to him.
npcs.goal: Wanted the station to stay a Pittman's for as long as the highway ran past it.
npcs.secret: He borrowed against the station from Harlan Voss in 1998 to get through a bad year, and that note, rolled over and over, is the one Carter Sturdivant holds on Royce now.
npcs.history: Clyde Pittman built the station in 1966, when the highway still brought the trucks through town, and ran it until the day he died at the pumps in 2009. His photo still hangs over the register.

npcs.name: Dale Purvis
npcs.where: the state penitentiary, eight years into a fifteen-year sentence
npcs.reach: letters, and a collect call on Sunday nights; visiting is the second and fourth Saturday
npcs.role: Wade's younger brother and Colt's father, in the state penitentiary
npcs.look: Lean, gray-stubbled man of forty-nine in prison whites, with his brother's face gone harder and a cross tattooed on the back of each hand.
npcs.voice: Talks fast on the phone because the call is timed, asks about the river before he asks about anyone, and never says goodbye, only later.
npcs.goal: Make parole in two years and come home to the job on the river his brother has promised him.
npcs.secret: He took the whole charge that sent him away, a trailer load of stolen outboard motors, so that Wade would not go down with him, and his letters have started asking what that bought him.
npcs.history: Dale ran the river with Wade from the time they were boys. He was sentenced in 2018 over a trailer load of stolen outboard motors and has done eight years of fifteen at the state penitentiary. Colt was fourteen when he went in.

npcs.name: Warren Pettit
npcs.where: Calder, at his engineering firm on the courthouse square
npcs.reach: by email to his firm; he has stopped taking calls about the bridge
npcs.role: the consulting engineer from Calder who wrote the report that condemned the old bridge
npcs.look: Soft, pale man of fifty-one in a pressed polo shirt with his firm's logo on it, rimless glasses and a hard hat that has never been dirty.
npcs.voice: Talks in percentages and section numbers, says per the report instead of yes, and ends every call by saying he has another one.
npcs.goal: Get through the council meeting without being asked a question under oath, and get paid for the downstream design work.
npcs.secret: He wrote most of the bridge report from Virgil Odom's answers on the phone and the state's old files, and spent inspection day at lunch with Carter Sturdivant instead of under the spans.
npcs.history: Warren Pettit runs a two-man engineering firm in Calder that does bridge and culvert work for the state. He inspected the old bridge in April, and his report rated it critical. He has not been back to Lockett's Ferry since.

npcs.name: Renee Byrd
npcs.where: Calder, where she cleans teeth at a dental office near the hospital
npcs.reach: her number is in Hollis's phone, and she lets it ring
npcs.role: Hollis's daughter, a dental hygienist in Calder
npcs.look: Tidy, dark-haired woman of thirty-eight in navy scrubs, with her father's heavy eyebrows and a ring she turns when she is nervous.
npcs.voice: Polite and final; says I'm not doing this with you today, and means it.
npcs.goal: Keep her own family clear of her father's business.
